translation: Let me now explain the rules of chess.
Let's now explain the special rule of castling.
Castling uses the king and the rook.
It's a special movement rule.

In order to castle, a few conditions must
have been met.

1. The king and the rook must not have moved
at all.

Neither the king nor the rook can have moved
since the start of the game.

As long as one of the rooks has not been
moved, it can be used for castling.
2. You must not be in check.
The king must not be in check.

In other words, this cannot be used as a
quick escape from check.

3. The king's movement range must not be
under attack by the opponent's pieces.

When castling, the king's movement range
must not intersect…
…with the enemy pieces' attack range.

4. There must not be any pieces between the
king and the rook.

There must not be any pieces obstructing
movement between the king and the rook…
…which will be used for castling.

If those four conditions are met, it is possible
to castle.

Castling is a special rule which makes the
king, which can usually only move one space…

…move two spaces and, at the same time,
causes the rook to move to its side.
It's a special movement rule.

Let's put it into practice.
Take a look at the bottom screen.

This is castling. It's the only move where you
can move two pieces at once.
You can also castle on the other side.

The distance the rook moves when castling on
the right is slightly different.
You can remember it as…

…the king moves two moves, and the rook
moves to its side.

We already explained it when covering the
castling conditions…

…but if the king's movement range is under
the enemy pieces' attack…
…you cannot castle.

Either defend with your ally pieces, or
eliminate the attacking piece before castling.
That concludes the explanation on castling.
